content.text:
Classification is working. `go run ./cmd/serve -kev` now serves TypeSafe's `POST /v1/systemone` on Vulkan, and its probabilities are within 4e-4 of Kev-4B's own fp32 output. The official TypeSafe Python SDK works against it unchanged. The plan is in `CLASSIFICATION.md` as K-stages: K0–K6 are done, and K7 (speed) and K8 (accuracy on a full test set) are open.

**What Jev and Kev are.** Jev (TypeSafe) takes one text and a set of typed questions, and answers each question with a probability distribution in a single forward pass, with no text generated. The questions share the text but can't see each other. Kev is the open version, built from Archer Hume's reverse-engineering of Jev. Kev-4B is `Qwen3.5-4B-Base` (a mix of DeltaNet and attention layers) plus a LoRA adapter and a small "pointer head" that scores each option against the question. The raw scores are then divided by a fitted temperature (2.41) to calibrate them.

**The details at the start that decide correctness.** Each of these gives a plausible but wrong model if misread:
- The yes/no question type really is spelled `noul`, in requests and responses.
- The markers between parts of the input are reused Qwen tokens in unexpected roles: the question's answer is read at `<|fim_suffix|>`, and each option is scored at `<|box_end|>`.
- A yes/no question is two options in the order `[no, yes]`, and the answer is p(yes).
- There is no start-of-text token. User text containing `<|name|>` is rewritten so it can't fake a marker.
- JSON is turned into text Python's way: key order kept, `2` and `2.0` rendered differently, `True`/`False`.

**How I checked it.** I copied Kev's own code into `reference/kev/` unchanged and ran it in fp32 as the reference, dumping four test requests. It agrees with itself two ways (via its cache and without it) to 3e-7.
- **Request layer:** tokens, positions, rendered text and the serialised answers are identical to Kev's.
- **GPU model:** every layer is within 2e-3 of the reference.
- **All questions in one pass:** within 4e-4 of Kev's probabilities, and no question's top answer changes. Kev's own bf16 server is about 0.03 from fp32.
- **Isolation:** rewriting or removing one question leaves every other answer exactly the same.
- **Over HTTP:** bad requests get 422, and a client that names no model is still answered.

**Changes to shared code:**
- **Tokenizer bug:** `zimage/tokenizer.Load` never read which splitting rule `tokenizer.json` asks for, and always used Qwen2's. That is silently wrong for Qwen3.5 on text with combining marks, such as Hindi. It now reads the rule and refuses ones it doesn't know. The existing users all use Qwen2's rule, and their tests still pass.
- **`safetensors`:** gained `File.Get` and `File.Names`.
- **`.venv`:** peft 0.21.0 is added there, for the reference run.

**Known gaps:**
- Non-NFC Unicode text still tokenises differently from Kev, the same gap as every tokenizer in the repo. A test pins it.
- A request larger than `-kev-tokens` (default 8192 tokens) is refused with a 422. Kev would split it across passes; that comes with the prefix cache in K7.

**Speed.** Kev's README example takes 64 ms here, against 41.5 ms on an L40S and 18.1 ms on an H100. At that size 90% of the time is reading the 7.1 GB of fp16 weights, so the next step is the int8 weight format the LLM already uses, which halves the bytes. The new kernels only start to matter on long texts.

Nothing is committed, and `-kev` isn't in `ai.service`. It would need about 9 GB on the small-verticals machine; your call on whether and when to deploy it.

| P1's attributed bank | 4.281 GB → 56.5 tok/s | **4.171 → 58.0** |

**And P1's "the router reads above the bus" is an artefact of the same row.**
The attribution put `moe_router` at 0.252 GB in 0.764 ms — 329.8 GB/s — and
*excluded it from the loss column* under D16 on the grounds that no DRAM
measurement can exceed 242. On the right byte count it is **0.1416 GB in
0.764 ms, 185 GB/s** (or 203 against the 0.697 ms the streaming dispatch
alone takes, with `moe.router.sum` counted separately). That is an ordinary
streaming rate, beside `deltanet`'s 201.5 and `moe.up`'s 200.6 — the router
is a normal member of the weight-streaming set and had been filed as an
anomaly.

### 1a. The same error, one row over, and it is the one that cost a stage

P1's table splits the expert traffic as **gate+up 1.003 GB and down 0.501** —
a 2:1 split, which is the ratio of their *parameters*. They do not have the
same width. gate and up are Q4_K (Q5_K on layer 2) at 4.52 bits; `down` is
Q5_1 on 43 layers and Q8_0 on five, **6.26 bits**. The bytes are:

    gate + up   2 x 40.265 B params at 4.52 bits = 45.49 GB  x 10/512 = 0.8886 GB/tok
    down            40.265 B params at 6.26 bits = 31.51 GB  x 10/512 = 0.6154

which sum to the 1.504 the inventory reports, as the 1.003/0.501 pair also
does. Re-read against P1's own milliseconds:

| family | GB/tok | ms | GB/s as printed | GB/s corrected |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| moe experts, gate+up | 1.003 → **0.889** | 4.998 | 200.6 | **177.8** |
| moe experts, down | 0.501 → **0.615** | 3.399 | 147.5 | **181.0** |
| moe_router | 0.252 → **0.142** | 0.764 | 329.8 | **185.3** |

**`moe.down` was never the outlier.** Its 147.5 GB/s — "60.9% of the bus,
+1.19 ms lost", the largest single item on P1's list after `hyper_conn` — is
arithmetic, not silicon: at the true byte count it reads at 181, *faster*
than the gate/up pair off the same bank. P1b spent a stage on it, re-screened
sixteen cold banks at one iteration, found that **no rung moves on any axis**,
and concluded "the 1.19 ms was the MALL's arithmetic". The null result was
right and its explanation was not: there was no 1.19 ms, because there was no
147.5 GB/s.

The lesson generalises past this table. **D16 says a rate above 242 GB/s was
not measuring DRAM; the rate is a quotient, and the numerator is as capable
of being wrong as the denominator.** Three of the nine rows in P1's table had
a byte count from a different source than the bank they were timing — two
from the checkpoint's widths and one from a parameter split — and each of
them landed on a rate that was read as a finding.

## 2. 640 is not a multiple of 256

The expert half of P4 asked for `ffn_down_exps` at Q4_K. Its dims are
`[640, 2560, 512]`: the reduction axis, the one a scale group and an
335:**And one of the three things L8e was scoped as was wrong, which is D16.** The
707:| ~~**P1b**~~ | ~~**`moe.down`'s rung, and the shared expert's**~~ — **done, and no rung moves.** The whole one-token MoE ladder in `l8e_moe.csv` was an L3 measurement — every GEMV down rung read 267-357 GB/s of a 242 GB/s bus — so it was re-run on **sixteen cold banks at `-iters 1`** (25.6 GB, so `ProfileSweep` never re-reads a bank warm). from kev.model import ContextOverflow
from kev.predictors import LocalPredictor, RemotePredictor, RotationAveraged
from kev.suite import CONTEXT, ENCODING, digest, load_split, read_manifest, record_digest, write_json


def labels(q):
    """(option keys, label index) of a labelled request question."""
    keys = question_keys(q["type"], q.get("criteria"))
    return keys, keys.index(q["label"]) if q["type"] == "choice" else int(q["label"])


def validate_distribution(raw, keys):
    if set(raw) != set(keys):
        raise ValueError("probability keys do not match requested options")
    p = np.array([raw[k] for k in keys], dtype=float)
    if not np.isfinite(p).all() or (p < 0).any() or (p > 1).any():
        raise ValueError("non-finite or out-of-range probabilities")
    total = float(p.sum())
    if total <= 0 or abs(total - 1) > max(1e-5, len(keys) * 0.005 + 1e-8):
        raise ValueError(f"invalid probability sum: {total}")
    return p / total, total


def prediction_rows(record, prediction):
    if set(prediction["probabilities"]) != set(record["questions"]):
        raise ValueError("answer IDs differ from request IDs")
    meta = record["_meta"]
    rows = []
    for qid, q in record["questions"].items():
        keys, y = labels(q)
        p, total = validate_distribution(prediction["probabilities"][qid], keys)
        row = {"id": meta["id"], "group": meta["group_id"], "question": qid,
               "source": meta["source"], "task": q["src"], "type": q["type"],
               "variant": meta["variant"], "keys": keys, "label": y, "control_id": meta.get("control_id"),
               "pair_id": meta.get("pair_id"), "sibling": meta.get("sibling"), # suites frozen before parent_id existed stored the parent's id in group_id for variants
               "parent": meta.get("parent_id") or (meta["id"] if meta["variant"] == "clean" else meta["group_id"]),
               "p": p.tolist(), "raw_probability_sum": total, "zero_count": int((p == 0).sum())}
        if "logits" in prediction:
            raw_logits = prediction["logits"][qid]
            if set(raw_logits) != set(keys) or not all(math.isfinite(raw_logits[k]) for k in keys):
                raise ValueError("logit keys or values do not match the requested options")
            row["logits"] = [float(raw_logits[k]) for k in keys]
            row["inference_temperature"] = prediction["inference_temperature"]
        rows.append(row)
    return rows


def summarize(rows, temperature=1.0, heldout_sources=()):
    """Report over benchmark rows. heldout_sources: sources the scored model never trained on; their tasks are also
    reported as a separate block."""
    clean = [r for r in rows if r["variant"] == "clean"]
    tasks = grouped_metrics(clean, "task")
    variants = grouped_metrics(rows, "variant")
    lookup = {(r["id"], r["question"]): r for r in clean}
    diffs, flips = [], []
    for row in rows:
        if row["variant"] == "permuted" and row["type"] == "choice":
            original = lookup[(row["parent"], row["question"])]
            aligned = [row["p"][row["keys"].index(k)] for k in original["keys"]]
            diffs.append(float(np.max(np.abs(np.array(aligned) - original["p"]))))
            flips.append(int(np.argmax(aligned) != np.argmax(original["p"])))

    return {"objective": -float(np.mean([v["nll"] for k, v in tasks.items() if not k.startswith("unknowable_") or k.startswith("unknowable_control")])),
            "paired_flip": paired_flip(clean), "unknowable": unknowable_report(clean),
            "clean": metrics(knowable), "tasks": tasks, "variants": variants,
            "heldout_tasks": grouped_metrics([r for r in clean if r["source"] in heldout_sources], "task") if any(r["source"] in heldout_sources for r in clean) else {},
            "permutation": {"n": len(diffs), "mean_max_delta": float(np.mean(diffs)) if diffs else None,

            "metric_policy": {"version": 2, "selective_ties": "whole_confidence_groups",
                              "coverage_at_error": "in-sample maximum over confidence thresholds; not a deployed error guarantee",
                              "aurc": "right-step integral over whole confidence groups",
                              "confident_error_rate": "high-confidence errors divided by all questions",
                              "error_rate_at_0_9": "errors divided by questions accepted at p_max >= 0.9",
                              "nll": "exact from logits when recorded; otherwise from floored probabilities",

                              "raw_sums_outside_1e_5": sum(abs(r["raw_probability_sum"] - 1) > 1e-5 for r in rows),
                              "returned_zeros": sum(r["zero_count"] for r in rows)}}


def predictions(records, predictor):
    """Yield, in record order, a zero-argument callable that returns predictor(record) or raises what it raised. A
    predictor with `concurrency` > 1 (RemotePredictor: one independent HTTP request per call) keeps that many calls in
    flight on a thread pool; in-process predictors (one GPU) have no `concurrency` and run one record at a time. Either

content.text:
The int8 bank is done and is now the default, but it's a 1.22–1.41x speedup on short requests, not the 2x the halved weight bytes suggested. The README ticket over HTTP went from 64 to 54 ms, and the weights shrank from 7.1 to 3.8 GB.

**Accuracy.** I scored Kev's `transfer-v4` development suite (764 questions) with a new `cmd/kev` tool that grades the way `kev.benchmark` does:

| | fp16 bank | int8 bank |
|---|---|---|
| accuracy, 656 clean questions | 0.8155 | 0.8140 |
| Kev's published fp32 | 0.817 | |
| argmax agreement with fp16 | | 762 / 764 |
| average time per record | 62.9 ms | 49.6 ms |

The two banks' probabilities differ by 0.0024 on average (worst 0.027). That's within the gap between Kev's own bf16 server and its fp32 numbers. The fp16 run also gives us most of K8: we land one question below Kev's published figure.

**Speed by pass length** (whole passes, best of three):

| tokens | int8 | fp16 | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 37 | 35.2 ms | 49.7 ms | 1.41x |
| 80 | 42.1 ms | 54.6 ms | 1.30x |
| 101 | 46.3 ms | 56.3 ms | 1.22x |
| 494 | 155.3 ms | 154.2 ms | 1.0x |

At a few hundred tokens the model is limited by arithmetic, not by reading weights, so the weight format stops mattering.

**Why not 2x.** The int8 GEMM kernel (the LLM's, reused unchanged) only reads weights at about 125 GB/s, while this machine sustains 180–200 GB/s for this kind of work. I built and timed three kernels of my own to close that gap: splitting the work along K, several waves sharing one converted weight slab, and loading the next slab during the current slab's math. Each one lost to the LLM's kernel at every length from 37 to 494 tokens. I deleted them rather than keep dead code, and recorded the measurements in `CLASSIFICATION.md` so nobody retries them. My best explanation is that the time goes to staging each slab through shared memory, which none of the three changed. A kernel that avoids that round trip is the next thing to try, not another rearrangement.

Batching 8 layers into each GPU submission saved only about 2 ms (53.1 → 51.9 ms), so that wasn't where the time went either.

**What else changed.** `-kev-fp16` (server) and `KEV_BANK=fp16` (tests) run the fp16 bank as a comparison. The single-row test's error bound is now set per bank from measurement: 2.8e-2 per layer for int8 against 2.0e-3 for fp16. All tests pass on both banks and `go vet ./...` is clean. `CLASSIFICATION.md`, `API.md`, `TODO.md` and my memory notes are updated. Nothing is committed.

Next in K7 is the state cache: when a request repeats a text, run only its questions. That is Kev's "same text again" speed column, and it also lets requests longer than `-kev-tokens` run in several passes instead of getting a 422. I'd take it before another attempt at the int8 kernel. Say if you'd rather have the kernel first.

content.text:
Starting K7.2. The design:
- **Working state.** After any pass that includes the state, the per-layer regions already hold its KV (cells `[0, Ls)`) and each GDN layer's final S. What's missing is the conv tail, so `kev_gdn_prep` will write the state's last three conv inputs. A **branch-only pass** can then run against that state, with `kStride = Ls`, no state scan, and the conv history read from the tail.
- **Cross-request cache.** A few fixed slots in their own buffer, keyed by the state's exact token ids, LRU. On a miss after a state pass, the state is copied into a slot; on a hit it's copied back. Both copies are GPU copy dispatches (host reads of these arenas run at 0.2 GB/s), about 60 MB for a short state.
- **Chunking.** A request longer than a pass runs its state alone, then its branches in groups that fit. That removes today's 422.

First the kernels: the tail write in `kev_gdn_prep`, and a copy kernel that sees the cache buffer.

content.text:
The prefix cache is done: a text the server has already seen is answered from saved state, with exactly the same bits as a fresh run. For a 2,269-token text with five questions, a repeat takes **130 ms instead of 1.4 s**. The same machinery also runs requests longer than `-kev-tokens` in several passes, so they no longer get a 422.

**What was built:**
- **Several kinds of pass.** A request now runs as the state plus the questions that fit, the state alone, or questions alone against the state left on the device. For the last kind, the DeltaNet kernel now saves the last three inputs of the text's convolution window.
- **Cache slots.** Four slots by default, each holding a text of up to 4,096 tokens (309 MB a slot, 1.2 GB in total). They are keyed by the text's exact token ids and evicted least-recently-used. Saving and restoring are GPU copies (`kev_copy.comp`), because the CPU reads these buffers at only ~0.2 GB/s. The server takes `-kev-cache` (0 turns it off) and `-kev-cache-tokens`.
- **Remaining 422s.** Only a text or a single question longer than one pass is still refused.

**Checks, on both weight formats:**
- A cache hit gives answers bit-identical to the first run, and eviction evicts the least-recently-used text.
- A request split across several passes gives answers bit-identical to one pass. Over HTTP I forced that with `-kev-tokens 384` on the 494-token fixture.
- The earlier question-isolation test now goes through cache hits and still passes.

**Against the speeds in Kev's README** (int8 weights, wall clock, best of three):

| | new text | same text again | Kev L40S | Kev H100 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 questions, short text | 76 ms | 74 ms | 41.5 / 27.7 | 18.1 / 12.9 |
| 5 questions, 2,269-token text | 1,425 ms | **130 ms** | 145 / 43 | 89 / 22.5 |

A short text gains almost nothing from the cache, because its cost is reading the weights, not the text. Over HTTP a 324-token text went from 169 to 80 ms on a repeat.

content.text:
The attention kernel is done. On a 2,439-token pass, attention drops from 549 to **106 ms** (5.2x), and a new 2,269-token text with five questions now takes **861 ms instead of 1.34 s**. A repeat of the same text takes **103 ms** (was 125). Accuracy against Kev is unchanged: the fixtures are within 0.0079 of Kev's fp32, with no changed answers.

**What was built.** `shaders/kev_attn_wmma.comp` is a flash attention on the matrix cores. One wave handles 16 query rows of one head, over blocks of 64 keys. Kev's mask is applied per row and key, because a group of 16 rows can straddle the text and a question, or two questions. Blocks that belong entirely to other questions are skipped. The attention's key/value cache moved to fp16, which halves a cached token to 32 KB (a cache slot is now 181 MB) and frees about 1 GB of working memory. The old one-key-at-a-time kernel stays as a comparison (`KEV_ATTN=naive`) and reads the same cache.

**Keeping answers exact.** The first version broke the guarantee that removing one question leaves the others' answers bit-identical (they moved by ~1e-4). This kind of attention groups keys into blocks, so when later questions shifted position their keys fell into different blocks. The fix: every question's keys now start on a 64-cell boundary, so a block holds only the text's keys or one question's. With that, **isolation and cache hits are bit-exact again on both weight formats**.

**One unexplained difference remains.** When the README ticket is split across passes in one particular way, one question moves by at most **2.5e-6**. That's far below the 4 decimals answers are reported to. The old kernel gives exact answers there. I ruled out three causes with tests I added:
- The key grouping above (now fixed).
- Padding rows leaking into matrix multiplies: no real output changes when padding is zeros, large values or NaN, on every kernel variant.
- Reading memory the pass never wrote: every temporary buffer is filled with NaN before each pass, and every answer stays finite.

I stopped there. The split-pass test allows 1e-5 for the new kernel and requires exactness for the old one. Along the way I also made the working buffer start zeroed and made the attention write only real rows.

**Where a long new text's time goes now** (848 ms of GPU time for 2,439 tokens):
- matrix multiplies, about 530 ms, running at ~34 TFLOPS;
- attention, 106 ms;
- the DeltaNet state scan, 81 ms.

The scan is the next step, K7.4. It's one thread per column walking the text token by token, and the LLM's scan kernel already shows how to split that work.

All tests pass in all three weight-format and attention combinations, and `go vet ./...` is clean. `CLASSIFICATION.md`, `API.md`, `TODO.md` and my memory notes are updated. Nothing is committed.

content.text:
The GDN scan is done. I rebuilt it in the shape the LLM vertical already measured as best on this machine, and it's **2.3x faster on a long text** (81 + 5 ms down to **35 + 2.6 ms** at 2,439 tokens) and faster at every length I measured. A new 2,269-token text now takes **821 ms** end to end (was 861), and 101 ms when repeated.

**What changed.** The old kernel gave one thread a whole 128-row column of the scan's running state and ran only 32 workgroups on a 40-CU GPU. Now 8 lanes share each column, each holding 16 of its values in registers and loading its own inputs every token, with no shared memory or barriers. Each head now runs as 16 workgroups instead of one. The segment handling (start from zero or from the state's saved result, optionally keep the final result) is unchanged.

**Timing by lanes per column** (state scan + question scans, all 24 layers, ms):

| tokens | old kernel | 1 | 2 | 4 | **8** | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 101 | 0.73 + 1.64 | 1.74 + 4.64 | 0.50 + 1.35 | 0.44 + 1.24 | **0.36 + 1.05** | 0.50 + 1.31 |
| 494 | 10.3 + 4.3 | 24.9 + 11.1 | 7.66 + 3.04 | 6.69 + 2.84 | **4.30 + 2.13** | 4.57 + 2.50 |
| 2,439 | 80.9 + 4.8 | 207.8 + 12.7 | 70.0 + 4.3 | 62.8 + 4.0 | **35.0 + 2.6** | 37.0 + 2.9 |

8 lanes wins everywhere, the same result the LLM found, so it's the default. `KEV_SCAN_LPC` selects another, and `TestGPUScanLadder` produces the table.

**Checks.**
- All tests pass with each weight format and attention kernel.
- Accuracy against Kev is unchanged (probabilities within 0.0078, no answer changes).
- `transfer-v4` dev is still **0.8140**. Every question gets the same top answer as the earlier int8 run (764 of 764), and a record now takes 46.5 ms (was 49.6).

**Where the time goes now.** A 2,439-token pass is 799 ms of GPU time:
- the matrix multiplies, 522 ms, at about 34 TFLOPS;
- attention, 102 ms;
- the DeltaNet prep kernel, 44 ms;
- the SwiGLU activation, 40 ms, which is just a memory-bound pass;
- the scan, 35 ms.

The scan still walks the text token by token. Going further needs the chunked form of the DeltaNet update, which is a different algorithm rather than a tweak.

The remaining sizeable levers are merging SwiGLU into the matrix multiply before it and improving the prep kernel, about 10% of a long pass together. Beyond that, the choice is between speed and the other open work:
- batching several requests into one pass (K7.5), which adds throughput rather than cutting latency;
- K8's row-by-row check against Kev's fp32 output.

Short requests like the README ticket (54 ms) are still limited by the int8 matrix multiply's read speed, which three earlier attempts didn't fix. `CLASSIFICATION.md`, `API.md`, `TODO.md` and my memory notes are updated, `go vet ./...` is clean, and nothing is committed.

content.text:
Two independent changes. First, the SwiGLU fusion. Today gate and up are two GEMMs that each write fp32 to memory, then a third pass reads both back and writes the fp16 input for `down`. The plan:
- **One interleaved weight.** Each 64-column group of the fused `[gate | up]` projection holds 32 gate rows then the matching 32 up rows, so one workgroup owns both halves of its outputs.
- **A GLU epilogue.** It computes `silu(g) · u` element-wise on the two accumulator tiles, which share a layout, and stores fp16 straight into `down`'s A operand.

That saves a whole pass, both fp32 writes, and a second read of A. It's the same fp32 formula on the same accumulators, so the answers should come out **bit-identical** to the unfused path. I'll do this on the int8 bank, the default; fp16 stays unfused as the control. The kernel is a Kev-owned copy of the LLM's int8 GEMM arm with only the epilogue changed.

content.text:
Both pieces are in. The bigger win came from something I found along the way rather than from the fusion itself: the order in which the GEMM visits the weights.

**SwiGLU fusion.** Gate and up are now one int8 GEMM with SwiGLU computed in its epilogue, writing fp16 straight into `down`'s input. That removes a whole pass and two fp32 writes. It applies to the int8 bank; the fp16 bank keeps the old path as the control. I had said the result would be bit-identical to the unfused path, and it isn't: two separately compiled shaders don't round the same expression identically. The difference is tiny (up to 0.0019 across the suite, every argmax the same).

**Grid order was the real problem.** The first fused version was *slower* than the three passes it replaced. The LLM's GEMM visits every weight column for the first block of rows before starting the second block. A weight matrix larger than the 32 MB last-level cache is therefore read from memory twice, once per row block. Gate or up alone fit in that cache; fused they don't, and neither does the input projection. My fused kernel now goes the other way round, finishing each column for all rows before moving on, and I added a plain version of it for the other projections. On the fused weight at 494 rows that's 1.81 → 1.26 ms per layer.

**A GEMM variant per projection.** Neither order wins everywhere, so each projection now uses whichever measured fastest for its shape at that request length (`TestGPUProjLadder` prices them). The column-by-column order wins for the wide input projection up to about 1,000 rows. The LLM's order still wins for the narrow `out` and `down` projections at every length, and for the input projection on long passes.

**GDN prep.** Only a small gain, 43.1 → 42.0 ms, from spreading the normalisation step across all threads. A rewrite giving each thread a contiguous run of channels was 5x slower because the memory reads stopped coalescing, so I reverted it. That result is recorded in the plan so nobody retries it.

**Where it lands:**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| GPU kernel time, 101-token request | 46.8 ms | **42.9 ms** |
| GPU kernel time, 494-token request | ~147 ms | **125.4 ms** |
| GPU kernel time, 2,439-token request | 799 ms | **744 ms** |
| 2,269-token text, new / again | 821 / 101 ms | **761 / 87 ms** |
| README ticket over HTTP, new / again | 54 ms | **51.9 / 45.8 ms** |
| transfer-v4 dev, per record | 46.5 ms | **45.0 ms** (accuracy still 0.8140, 764/764 argmax agreement) |

I also found that the GEMM speed test had been timing cache hits ever since the state cache went in. It now clears the cache before each run.

All tests pass across both weight formats and both attention kernels, and `go vet ./...` is clean. `CLASSIFICATION.md`, `API.md`, `TODO.md` and my memory notes are updated. Nothing is committed.

A long request is now about 70% GEMMs, running at roughly 35 TFLOPS. What's left is batching several requests into one pass (K7.5, which adds throughput rather than cutting latency) or the row-by-row comparison against Kev's fp32 output for K8.

Starting K7.5. I'm at 75% context, so I'll keep tool output short. The design:
- **Per-request state slots.** Each request in a pass gets its own GDN S and conv tail (a slot of the GDN block) and its own attention cells, each request's state starting on a 64-aligned cell.
- **Richer per-row metadata** (8 words): position, state-or-branch, segment start row, own cell, the request's state cell range, its slot, and where its state ends in this pass. The attention mask becomes `key ≤ cell && (key ∈ [sLo, sHi) || key ≥ lo)`, so it no longer needs a single global state.
- **Scan segments carry a slot.** One dispatch runs every state in the pass, then one runs every branch, each reading its own request's S.
- **Cache copies take a slot and a base cell**, so a hit restores into whichever slot its request got.
- **A batcher in the backend** takes whatever is queued, up to a cap, and runs it as one pass.

content.text:
Batching is done: concurrent requests now share GPU passes, and a request arriving alone waits for nothing. Sixteen concurrent short requests over HTTP run at **~29 per second**, against 19.5 per second one after another. One catch: with the default matrix-core attention, a request's probabilities shift very slightly depending on which other requests share its pass (details below).

**How it works.**
- **Per-request state.** Each request in a pass gets its own slot for the DeltaNet state (8 slots, 52.7 MB each), and its own region of the attention cache starting on a 64-aligned cell.
- **Per-row metadata.** Every row now records which request's state it may see and which slot it uses. The attention mask, the convolution history and the state scan all read from that, instead of assuming one shared state.
- **The cache.** A cached text is restored into whichever slot its request lands in.
- **The server.** One worker takes whatever requests are queued when the GPU frees up, at most `-kev-batch` (default 8), and runs them as one pass. `cmd/kev -batch N` does the same for a test suite.

**Results:**

| | one at a time | batched |
|---|---|---|
| 8 short requests (test) | 401 ms | **266 ms** (1.51x) |
| transfer-v4 dev, per record | 45.0 ms | **27.3 ms** (1.65x) |
| 16 concurrent HTTP requests | 822 ms, 19.5/s | **553 ms, 28.9/s** |
| 1 HTTP request | 52 ms | 55 ms |

**Accuracy.** Batched, transfer-v4 dev scores **0.8140**, and all 764 answers match the unbatched run. With the simple attention kernel, batched results are bit-exact in every case I tried: cold, all cached, and half cached. With the default matrix-core attention, probabilities shift by up to **6e-4** (mean 3e-5) depending on which requests share the pass. It's the same effect as last round's unexplained residue, just larger here. Forcing a single matrix-multiply variant doesn't change it, and switching to the simple kernel removes it, so the cause is somewhere in how the matrix-core kernel's work is grouped. Kev's own batched server makes the same promise ("up to floating-point reassociation"). The batch test holds the matrix-core kernel to 1e-3 and the simple kernel to exact equality.

**A bug I caused and fixed.** Rows now carry 8 words of metadata instead of 4, and segments 4 words instead of 2. I hadn't enlarged their buffers, so the first batch overran them and hung the GPU. Both are now sized for the new layout.

All tests pass with both weight formats and both attention kernels, and `go vet ./...` is clean. `CLASSIFICATION.md`, `API.md`, `TODO.md` and my memory notes are updated. Nothing is committed. `-kev` still isn't in `ai.service`; it's ready for the small-verticals machine whenever you want it deployed.

What's left: K8's row-by-row comparison against Kev's own fp32 output, and tracking down that matrix-core attention residue. Separately, a long request is now about 70% matrix multiplies, and the README ticket (52 ms) is still held back by how fast the int8 matrix multiply reads its weights.
